description.value: The study investigated whether simple multiplication processing differed between the language in which bilingual adults learned multiplication and their other language, using behavioral measures and fMRI-defined language and quantity regions.

design.value: Thirty-five Spanish-English bilingual adults were recruited, six were excluded, and the final sample comprised 29 participants. Participants completed two localizer tasks and a single-digit multiplication verification task in one experimental session, with the verbal localizer and multiplication task administered in English and Spanish and language order alternated across participants.

description.value: Thirty-five Spanish-English bilingual adults were recruited; six initial participants were excluded and the final sample comprised 29 participants. All participants reported Spanish as their native language, with 8 also reporting English as a simultaneous native language. Eleven individuals learned multiplication in Spanish and 18 learned multiplication in English.

task_description.value: Participants heard two spoken number words, followed by a visual Arabic digit, and determined whether the Arabic digit was the correct product of the two spoken numbers. Two runs were presented in English and two runs in Spanish, with 36 multiplication problems and 12 control trials per run.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to determine whether the Arabic digit was the correct product of the two spoken numbers; they used their index finger if the proposed solution was true and their middle finger if the proposed solution was false.

stimuli.value: Two spoken number words followed by a visual Arabic digit; the spoken number words were presented in English or Spanish, and participants did not see any written words.

task_description.value: Participants saw a black-and-white line drawing of an object followed by a spoken word and determined whether the word matched the presented picture. Two runs were completed in English and two in Spanish.

instructions.value: Participants determined whether the spoken word matched the presented picture; they used their index finger if the picture-word pairs matched and their middle finger if they did not match.

stimuli.value: Black-and-white line drawings followed by spoken words in English or Spanish; mismatched trials differed across languages to avoid predictability.

task_performance_measures.value: behavioral responses for matched and mismatched trials

task_description.value: Participants determined which of two sequentially presented dot arrays contained more dots. Two runs were completed, with easy, medium, and hard comparisons and control trials.

instructions.value: Participants were tasked with determining which of two sequentially presented dot arrays contained more dots.

stimuli.value: Sequentially presented dot arrays with easy comparisons at a ratio of 1:3, medium comparisons at a ratio of 1:2, and hard comparisons at a ratio of 2:3; dot size was controlled across arrays.

task_performance_measures.value: behavioral responses indicating which dot array contained more dots

Functional images were realigned to their mean functional image across runs, co-registered to a skull-stripped anatomical image, normalized to the standard T1 Montreal Neurological Institute template, smoothed with a 6 mm isotropic Gaussian kernel, and processed with Art-Repair to identify and repair outlier volumes.

steps.value: All functional images were realigned to their mean functional image across runs.
An anatomical brain mask was created by combining grey matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid segmentation products.
The anatomical brain mask was applied to the original anatomical image to produce a skull-stripped anatomical image.
The mean functional image and all functional images were co-registered to the skull-stripped anatomical image.
All functional images were normalized to the standard T1 Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template.
Smoothing was applied to all functional images with a 6 mm isotropic Gaussian kernel.
Art-Repair was used to identify outlier volumes.
Outlier volumes were repaired by interpolation between the nearest non-outlier volumes.
Six motion parameters estimated during realignment were entered in the first-level modeling as regressors, and repaired volumes were deweighted.

model_settings.value: Activation was modeled as epochs time-locked to the first stimulus in each trial; all proposed solutions and all participants’ responses were included; time series data were high-pass filtered at 1/128 Hz; serial correlations were corrected using an autoregressive AR model; six realignment motion parameters were included as regressors and repaired volumes were deweighted.

Subjects were included as a random effect. Satterthwaite’s method was used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom for F statistics. Response time analyses included only trials with accurate responses.

LA+ vocabulary fluency was entered as a covariate of no interest and LA- vocabulary fluency as the independent variable; analyses were conducted separately for small and large problems and for accuracy and response time, and separately for brain activation in the regions of interest.

Brain data were modeled based on Problem Size, Language, and the additive effect with and without the interaction between the two. WAIC was used for model comparison, and posterior summaries provided Bayesian p-values; p-values were considered significant when the 95% highest posterior density for each parameter did not contain 0.
